title: How does a token bucket let a burst through but refuse a flood?
answer: A burst can spend only the tokens saved up, and only elapsed time adds more

checks.question: R6 is refused at all three rates. Would a faster refill or a bigger bucket let it through, and why?
checks.answer: A bigger bucket. R1 to R6 arrive at the same instant, so no time passes and refill adds nothing at any rate. A bucket of six tokens, still at 2 a second, answers R6 with 200.

checks.question: At 2 tokens a second, a client sends one request every 0.4 seconds from a full bucket and never pauses. Is any request refused, and what share gets through in the long run?
checks.answer: Yes. Each gap earns 0.8 tokens and each request spends one, so the saved five drain by 0.2 a request and request 22 is the first refused. From then on 80 of every 100 get through, 2 a second: the refill rate, however long the flood lasts.

checks.question: Suppose R10 arrived at 1.5 s instead of 5 s. At which of the three rates would it be refused?
checks.answer: At 1 token a second only. At 1 a second R9 leaves 0 and R10 finds 0.5; at 2 a second R9 leaves 0 and R10 finds 1; at 4 a second R9 leaves 1 and R10 finds 3. Half a second has to earn the token R9 did not leave.

scenarios.name: Refill per second: 1 token
invariants: the bucket stands where the balance line ends

steps.title: Ten requests from one client, and a bucket of five tokens
steps.line: Predict: R1–R6 arrive at the same instant. How many get 200?
steps.caption: A server shares its work among many clients, so it limits each one: a request it serves gets 200, OK, and one it refuses gets 429, Too Many Requests, which tells the client to slow down. A short burst, such as the requests a page makes as it loads, should still get through. So the server keeps a balance for the client of at most five tokens: the bucket. Each accepted request spends one token, and a request that finds less than one, under the 1 token line, gets 429. Ten requests will arrive at the times written above their boxes.
steps.picture: Bucket balance: 5 tokens left, last refill at 0 seconds, 0 accepted; rejected requests: none; The bucket, filled to 5.0 of 5 tokens; A chart of tokens, 0 to 5, against time, 0 to 5 s, with a dashed line at the one token a request needs; Requests R1 to R10 at their arrival times: none answered yet; Code “bucket.allow(now), rate = 1”, 8 lines. Refill: 2: tokens = min(5; 3: tokens + (now - lastRefill) * rate); 4: lastRefill = now.

steps.title: Answer: five 200s, then a 429
steps.line: Predict: R7 arrives half a second later, at 0.5 s. 200 or 429?
steps.caption: No time passed between R1 and R6, so the line drops one token per request and R6 finds 0.0, under the 1 token line: 429. A burst can spend only the tokens saved up, and only elapsed time adds more. On each arrival the server adds elapsed time multiplied by the refill rate, here 1 token a second, before deciding whether to spend a token. The line between arrivals shows available credit; no background timer needs to update the balance.
steps.picture: Bucket balance: 0 tokens left, last refill at 0 seconds, 5 accepted; rejected requests: R6; The bucket, filled to 0.0 of 5 tokens; A chart of the balance over time: it climbs at 1 a second between calls and drops one token for each 200. Dots mark what R1–R6 found; R6 at 0.0 is under the one-token line and got 429; Requests R1 to R10 at their arrival times: 5 answered 200, R6 429, 4 waiting; Code “bucket.allow(now), rate = 1”, 8 lines. Refuse: 5: if (tokens < 1) return 429. New in this step: Bucket balance: 0 tokens left, last refill at 0 seconds, 5 accepted; rejected requests: R6; The bucket, filled to 0.0 of 5 tokens; A chart of the balance over time: it climbs at 1 a second between calls and drops one token for each 200. Dots mark what R1–R6 found; R6 at 0.0 is under the one-token line and got 429; and 1 more.

steps.title: Answer: 429. R7 finds 0.5 tokens after half a second
steps.line: R8 at 1 s finds 1.0; R9 at the same instant finds what R8 left.
steps.caption: Between calls the line climbs 1 token a second. Half a second after the burst, R7 finds 0.5 tokens, less than the one a request needs, so it gets 429. The rate decides it: the same half second buys 0.5 tokens at 1 a second (429), 1.0 token at 2 a second (200) and 2.0 tokens at 4 a second (200). R8 at 1 s finds 1.0; R9 arrives at the same instant, so nothing is added and it finds what R8 left. Fractional tokens are saved, but a request must spend a whole one. R7 (0.5) and R9 (0.0) are under the 1 token line, so they get 429.

Dots mark what R1–R9 found; R6 at 0.0, R7 at 0.5 and R9 at 0.0 are under the one-token line and got 429; Requests R1 to R10 at their arrival times: 6 answered 200, R6, R7 and R9 429, 1 waiting; Code “bucket.allow(now), rate = 1”, 8 lines. Refuse: 5: if (tokens < 1) return 429. Dots mark what R1–R9 found; R6 at 0.0, R7 at 0.5 and R9 at 0.0 are under the one-token line and got 429; Requests R1 to R10 at their arrival times: 6 answered 200, R6, R7 and R9 429, 1 waiting.

steps.title: R10 waits 4 s and finds 4 tokens
steps.line: The line climbs to 4.0, under the cap of five.
steps.caption: R9 left 0, and a wait of 4 s at 1 token a second brings the balance to 4, under min(5, …)'s cap. R10 spends one and leaves 3. At 2 tokens a second and 4 tokens a second the same wait would pass five, and min(5, …) would stop the balance there.
steps.picture: Bucket balance: 3 tokens left, last refill at 5 seconds, 7 accepted; rejected requests: R6, R7, R9; The bucket, filled to 3.0 of 5 tokens; A chart of the balance over time: it climbs at 1 a second between calls and drops one token for each 200. Dots mark what R1–R10 found; R6 at 0.0, R7 at 0.5 and R9 at 0.0 are under the one-token line and got 429; Requests R1 to R10 at their arrival times: 7 answered 200, R6, R7 and R9 429; Code “bucket.allow(now), rate = 1”, 8 lines. Spend: 6: tokens -= 1; 7: return 200. New in this step: Bucket balance: 3 tokens left, last refill at 5 seconds, 7 accepted; rejected requests: R6, R7, R9; The bucket, filled to 3.0 of 5 tokens; A chart of the balance over time: it climbs at 1 a second between calls and drops one token for each 200. Dots mark what R1–R10 found; R6 at 0.0, R7 at 0.5 and R9 at 0.0 are under the one-token line and got 429; and 1 more.

steps.title: The same ten requests at 1, 2 and 4 tokens a second
steps.line: 429s at 4 / s: R6; at 1 / s: R6, R7 and R9.
steps.caption: Each row runs the same ten requests at its labelled refill rate; the outlined row is this scenario. Circles are 200s and crosses are 429s. R6 is refused at every rate, because no time passes inside the burst, and R10 is accepted at every rate, because after its 4-second wait it finds at least 4 tokens. Those are the three rates offered here; below a fifth of a token a second, R10 too would find less than one token. For R7 to R9 the rate decides: at 4 tokens a second none of them is refused; at 1 token a second R7 and R9 are refused. The bucket’s capacity sets the burst, and its rate sets how soon the client can send again.
steps.picture: Requests R1 to R10, left to right. 1 / s: R6, R7 and R9 get 429; all other requests get 200. 2 / s: R6 and R9 get 429; all other requests get 200. 4 / s: R6 gets 429; all other requests get 200. The 1 / s row is outlined.
